title: Episode 229: Poland-Lithuania: The Commonwealth of Nobles, the Liberum Veto, and the Three Partitions
description:
The tragic downfall of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth: the unique democracy of nobles, the fatal paralysis of the Liberum Veto, the heroic resistance of Tadeusz Kościuszko, and the erasure of a great nation from the map of Europe.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. Today, we turn to one of the most poignant and cautionary tragedies in European history: how the largest and freest kingdom of Central Europe, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, was paralyzed by extreme aristocratic liberty and devoured by the predatory absolute monarchies of Russia, Prussia, and Austria.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE GOLDEN LIBERTY: EUROPE'S FIRST NOBLE REPUBLIC
In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, while Western Europe was succumbing to royal absolutism and divine right of kings, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth developed a radical system of aristocratic democracy known as 'Golden Liberty'. Ten percent of the population belonged to the nobility, or szlachta—an extraordinarily broad political class compared to other European nations. The szlachta elected their monarchs in open-air gatherings outside Warsaw, forcing every royal candidate to sign the Henrician Articles, which strictly guaranteed religious tolerance, freedom from arbitrary arrest, and the absolute supremacy of parliament, the Sejm. Every nobleman, regardless of whether he owned a hundred villages or plowed his own small plot of rye with a rusty sword strapped to his belt, considered himself the equal of any king or duke. It was an idealistic noble commonwealth that outlawed religious warfare while the rest of Europe burned in the Thirty Years' War, fostering a proud chivalric culture of Sarmatism that celebrated Slavic independence and equestrian valor. In an era of royal tyranny, Poland-Lithuania offered a dazzling vision of constitutional freedom that was centuries ahead of its time. The szlachta gathered in the tens of thousands on the fields of Wola to cast their votes for the crown, deliberating on horseback with sabers drawn in a spectacular outdoor parliament of free citizens.  The szlachta's dedication to republican liberty was unmatched, considering their commonwealth a direct spiritual descendant of the ancient Roman Republic.  The Sarmatian dress of the Polish nobility—rich silk kontusz coats, ornate gold sashes, and curved sabers—stood in sharp contrast to the French wigs and powdered faces of Western European courts.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE FATAL CURSE OF THE LIBERUM VETO
Yet this radical devotion to individual freedom contained the fatal constitutional poison that would destroy the nation: the principle of unanimity known as the Liberum Veto. Based on the ideological conviction that no free nobleman could ever be bound by a majority vote against his conscience, the Liberum Veto permitted any single deputy in the Sejm to stand up, shout 'Nie pozwalam!'—'I do not permit!'—and instantly dissolve the entire legislative session, nullifying every single law, tax, and military appropriation passed during that session. Foreign powers—Russia, Prussia, and Austria—quickly recognized that they did not need to conquer Poland on the battlefield; they only needed to bribe a single disgruntled or corrupt deputy to shout 'Nie pozwalam!' and paralyze the entire government. For nearly a century, the Polish parliament was systematically rendered impotent: while neighboring powers built massive, centralized standing armies of hundreds of thousands of soldiers, the Commonwealth could not raise taxes to pay its own garrison or repair its frontier fortresses. The noble republic had become an ungovernable anarchy surrounded by hungry wolves. Between 1652 and 1764, out of eighty-eight parliamentary sessions convened in Warsaw, fifty-three were exploded and dissolved by the shout of a single deputy, leaving the state treasury empty and the army unfunded.  Neighboring absolute monarchs systematically bribed venal Lithuanian and Polish deputies with pensions, diamonds, and estates to paralyze the Warsaw parliament.  The principle of 'Nemine captivabimus'—guaranteeing that no nobleman could be imprisoned without a judicial trial—was established in Poland three centuries before the British Habeas Corpus Act.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE FIRST PARTITION: 1772
By 1772, the predatory empires surrounding Poland decided the time was ripe to carve up the defenseless commonwealth. Empress Catherine the Great of Russia, King Frederick the Great of Prussia, and Empress Maria Theresa of Austria met in secret to sign the First Partition of Poland. Together, they sliced off one-third of Poland's territory and half of its population, with Prussia annexing royal Prussia, Russia seizing the eastern borderlands, and Austria taking Galicia. In Warsaw, the Sejm was surrounded by Russian troops, who threatened the deputies with exile to Siberia if they did not ratify the dismemberment of their own homeland. One heroic deputy, Tadeusz Rejtan, tore open his shirt at the threshold of the parliamentary chamber, threw himself onto the floor, and cried out in agony: 'Trample me, kill me, but do not kill the Fatherland!' But the terrified deputies stepped over his weeping body and signed the treaty. The First Partition delivered a profound moral shock to Polish society, awakening a patriotic reform movement that recognized that the nation must radically modernize its political system or face complete annihilation. The loss of five million citizens and vital Baltic trade routes ignited an intellectual renaissance in Warsaw, as patriotic philosophers, journalists, and educators resolved to rescue the commonwealth through moral and constitutional renewal.  The First Partition shocked the European Enlightenment, demonstrating that international law and treaties offered zero protection against imperial greed.  The three partitioning powers justified their territorial robbery with cynical diplomatic manifestos claiming that Poland was an anarchic failed state that threatened the tranquility of its neighbors.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE CONSTITUTION OF MAY 3, 1791: A BEACON OF LIBERTY
In response to the national catastrophe, Polish patriots and intellectuals embarked upon the most daring constitutional reform movement in European history. Convening the Four-Year Sejm, leaders like King Stanisław August Poniatowski, Ignacy Potocki, and Hugo Kołłątaj worked in secret to draft a modern, revolutionary governing charter. On May 3, 1791, amidst cheering crowds filling the streets of Warsaw, the Sejm proclaimed the Constitution of May 3—the first written democratic national constitution in Europe, and the second in world history after the United States. The Constitution abolished the disastrous Liberum Veto forever, established a hereditary constitutional monarchy, created separation of executive, legislative, and judicial powers, granted political rights to townspeople, and placed the long-suffering peasantry under the protection of national law. Thomas Jefferson hailed the Polish Constitution as an extraordinary achievement of human enlightenment. But across the border in St. Petersburg, Catherine the Great viewed this flourishing democratic constitutionalism on Russia's western frontier as a dangerous, infectious disease that had to be exterminated immediately. The historic document was carried through the sunlit streets of Warsaw to the Cathedral of St. John, where the King and deputies swore a solemn oath before God to defend the new charter of freedom with their lives.  The Four-Year Sejm was accompanied by passionate political debates in Warsaw's coffeehouses, where reformist broadsheets and pamphlets were devoured by thousands of educated citizens.  King Stanisław August was a patron of the arts and sciences who transformed Warsaw into a neoclassical cultural capital, holding famous 'Thursday Dinners' with leading Polish writers and scholars.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SECOND PARTITION AND THE BETRAYAL OF TARGOWICA
Catherine the Great conspired with a reactionary clique of conservative Polish magnates who formed the Confederation of Targowica, declaring that the May 3 Constitution was an attack on traditional noble liberty. Catherine dispatched an army of one hundred thousand Russian troops into Poland to crush the constitutional government. Despite heroic resistance by the newly organized Polish army under Prince Józef Poniatowski and Tadeusz Kościuszko, the Commonwealth was overwhelmed by sheer numbers and betrayed by its supposed Prussian allies. In 1793, Russia and Prussia executed the Second Partition, stripping Poland of another massive swath of territory and reducing the once-mighty commonwealth to a tiny, crippled rump state of barely four million people, garrisoned by Russian troops. The reformist constitution was formally abolished at gunpoint, and the Polish nation seemed brought to the brink of the grave. Russian garrisons occupied Warsaw and provincial fortresses, while Polish officers who had fought for the constitution were stripped of their ranks, their estates confiscated by imperial decree.  Catherine the Great declared that the Polish constitution was a dangerous Jacobin contagion that threatened the monarchical order of Central Europe.  The betrayal of Targowica became an eternal symbol of national treason in Poland, leading several of its aristocratic ringleaders to be hanged in effigy by enraged mobs in Warsaw during the uprising.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE KOŚCIUSZKO UPRISING: THE SCYTHEMEN OF RACŁAWICE
Refusing to let their nation die without a fight, Polish patriots turned to the hero of the American Revolution: General Tadeusz Kościuszko. On March 24, 1794, in the main market square of Kraków, Kościuszko drew his sword before a crowd of thousands and took a solemn oath as Supreme Commander of the National Armed Forces, dedicating his life to the liberation of Poland. Lacking muskets and cannons, Kościuszko mobilized thousands of Polish peasants who forged their agricultural scythes vertically onto wooden poles, creating terrifying, razor-sharp polearms. At the Battle of Racławice, these peasant 'scythemen' charged bare-chested through heavy Russian cannon fire, overrunning Russian artillery batteries in an act of breathtaking valor. Kościuszko issued the Połaniec Manifesto, granting civil liberty to the peasantry and reducing feudal labor burdens, uniting nobles and peasants in common defense of the motherland. For seven thrilling months, the insurgent Polish forces held Warsaw against combined Russian and Prussian sieges, electrifying freedom-lovers across Europe. Kościuszko wore the simple peasant coat of grey homespun wool, demonstrating that in the hour of supreme danger, the peasant and the prince stood as equal brothers in the defense of human liberty.  Kościuszko's military engineers fortified the earthen ramparts of Warsaw with ingenious defensive redoubts, repelling combined Prussian and Russian assaults with deadly accuracy.  At the Battle of Szczekociny, Kościuszko fought with desperation against combined Russian and Prussian armies, having two horses shot from beneath him as he led infantry bayonet charges.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE THIRD PARTITION AND THE NATION THAT REFUSED TO DIE
In October 1794, the uprising met its tragic end: at the Battle of Maciejowice, Kościuszko was wounded by Cossack sabers and taken prisoner, while Russian forces under General Alexander Suvorov stormed the Warsaw suburb of Praga, massacring twenty thousand civilians. In 1795, the three imperial powers executed the Third Partition of Poland, carving up the remaining fragments of the country and signing a secret treaty pledging to eliminate the very name of the Kingdom of Poland from the historical record forever. King Stanisław August was forced to abdicate, and Poland vanished from the political map of Europe for one hundred and twenty-three years. Yet the soul of the nation proved indestructible. In exile, Polish legionnaires fighting in Italy composed a passionate military march that became the national anthem: 'Poland has not yet perished, so long as we still live!' Through a century of brutal imperial oppression, underground schools, heroic uprisings, and peerless romantic literature, the Polish people kept the flame of liberty burning, until the ashes of World War I saw the triumphant rebirth of a free Polish Republic in 1918. Across more than a century of partition, the Polish people preserved their language, their Catholic faith, and their unyielding devotion to liberty, proving that an empire may erase a nation's borders, but it can never extinguish the soul of a free people.  When Napoleon invaded Russia in 1812, nearly one hundred thousand Polish soldiers marched under the imperial eagles, hoping to resurrect their dismembered homeland.  The heroic memory of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth inspired nineteenth-century romantic poets like Adam Mickiewicz to write epic verses that preserved the national consciousness through generations of foreign occupation.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, we turn our gaze to the maritime lowlands of Western Europe with Episode 230: The Netherlands Part 1—William the Silent, the Dutch Revolt, and the Sea Beggars. Until then, stay curious.
